newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FORECAST - Goldman Sachs sees better Asian exports.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Goldman Sachs sees better Asian exports.

text.p: The general outlook for Asian exports remains bright, but there are few signs of sparkle in early 1997, Goldman Sachs said in its quarterly Asian outlook.
"Asian exports have generally posted a disappointing performance in early 1997," Goldman Sachs said.
Export recovery has been patchy. Exports from newly industrialised economies (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong) declined in the first-quarter, while ASEAN exports put in a more mixed performance.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Thailand continued to lag, while the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia reported stronger January exports. Thailand's exports declined 1.5 percent in February from 5.1 percent growth in January, the first positive figures in seven months.
At the other end of the spectrum, the Philippines bucked the trend with 16 percent growth over the first two months.
Indonesia's non-oil exports were up 13 percent in January against 3.4 percent in the fourth quarter, and Malaysian exports grew four percent in January after a flat fourth quarter.

The trend in composition of Asian exports does not reveal any difficulties shifting into higher value-added sectors, suggesting that the problem remains cyclical rather than structural, Goldman Sachs said.

But cyclical factors also provide little explanation for the weakness. Data suggests little systematic response of exports to changes in real effective exchange rates. And economic growth in Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) states is on the rise, suggesting demand should be improving.

Projected OECD growth of 2.4 percent in 1997 against 2.3 percent in 1996 indicates a volume increase in newly industrialised economies (NIEs) exports to 12 percent this year from 9.9 percent last year, and a rise in ASEAN exports to 7.5 percent this year from a 0.3 percent decline last year.

However, a closer examination of the data suggests that export value responds more sharply than export volume to OECD growth, which implies that export prices accentuate swings in Asian export performance.
Goldman Sachs argues that while the general outlook for Asian export remains bright, the outlook for export prices is less encouraging.
"This is particularly germane to explaining sluggishness in Asian exports, especially in the NIEs," Goldman said.
Weak inflation will prevent any appreciable uptake in Asian export prices, especially for the NIEs, Goldman said.

And although baseline forecasts project the decline in prices will trough by mid-1997 for key items such as electronics and machinery equipment, the base effect should mitigate against any appreciable recovery until the second half of the year.
The export price decline for the NIEs is expected to bottom out in the first quarter of 1997 at a decline of 9.2 percent, stabilising to a decline of 0.5 percent by fourth-quarter 1997.
"This, combined with our projection of export volumes yields an export value growth forecast of 6.5 percent for 1997 against three percent for 1996," Goldman said.

For ASEAN, export value growth is expected to remain flat in the first half before picking up to 3.2 percent in the second half. This implies value growth of 10.5 percent this year against 4.6 percent in 1996.
